title: Choosing the right average
summary: Which of mean, median and mode to use for which kind of data, with the pros, cons, examples and common mistakes.

chunks.heading: Which measure for which data type
chunks.explanation_md:
The tree on the slide matches data types to measures:
- **Nominal** (qualitative): **mode** only.
- **Ordinal** (qualitative): **mode and median**.
- **Discrete and continuous** (quantitative): **mode, median and mean**.

**Pros and cons:**
- **Mean:** takes all values into account, sensitive and reliable; but **biased in the presence of extreme values**.
- **Median:** not affected by extreme values; but **less sensitive than the mean**.
- **Mode:** the **only way to represent nominal data**; not affected by extreme values and works for qualitative data; but it can take **multiple values or no value at all**, and is less sensitive than the mean.
chunks.exam_line: Nominal: mode. Ordinal: mode, median. Quantitative: mode, median, mean. Mean is biased by extremes; median and mode are not.

chunks.heading: When to use each, with the professor's examples
chunks.explanation_md:
**Mean:** use when data is **symmetric, outliers are absent and all values matter**. It uses every value and is necessary for further analysis such as standard deviation. Weakness: sensitive to outliers. Example: if the CEO earns ₹10 crore and others average ₹6 lakh, the mean salary could mislead stakeholders.

**Median:** use when data is **skewed or has significant outliers**. It is not influenced by extremes, but does not use all values. Example: **median home price** is used by realtors because it is not inflated by a few luxury homes.

**Mode:** use for **categorical data** or when finding the "most popular" matters. Weakness: may have more than one mode, or none. Examples: in fashion retail the most sold t-shirt size guides inventory purchases; in a restaurant the mode meal helps design new combos.

**Choosing quickly:** employees' salaries (skewed, most earn ₹40k but the CEO ₹8L): **median**. Best-selling product size (size M t-shirts): **mode**. Daily sales in a stable market (a supermarket with consistent sales): **mean**.

**Common mistakes:** reporting the mean when outliers are present; ignoring multiple modes that matter for production planning; not saying which average is used in reports.
chunks.exam_line: Mean: symmetric, no outliers. Median: skewed or outliers. Mode: categorical or most popular. Mistakes: mean with outliers, ignoring multiple modes, not stating which average.

questions.stem: A shop owner wants to decide how many of each t-shirt size to stock. Which measure would you use and why?
questions.model_answer_md: Use the **mode**. The most sold t-shirt size (mode) guides inventory purchases, because it shows the most frequent occurrence. The mode suits categorical data such as size. Check whether there is more than one mode, as that would matter for the stocking plan.

rubric.point: Shows most frequent occurrence guiding inventory

questions.stem: Explain how to choose between mean, median and mode, using the deck's examples for each, and mention the common mistakes.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** The right average depends on the data type and on whether outliers are present.

**By data type.** Nominal: mode. Ordinal: mode and median. Quantitative (discrete or continuous): mode, median and mean.

**Mean.** Use when data is symmetric, outliers are absent and all values matter. It uses every value and is needed for further analysis such as standard deviation, but is sensitive to outliers. Example: if the CEO earns ₹10 crore and others average ₹6 lakh, the mean could mislead stakeholders.

**Median.** Use when data is skewed or has significant outliers. Example: median home price, not inflated by a few luxury homes.

**Mode.** Use for categorical data or the most popular item. Example: the most sold t-shirt size guides inventory; the mode meal helps a restaurant design combos.

**Common mistakes.** Mean with outliers; ignoring multiple modes; not stating which average.

**Conclusion.** Match the measure to the data and state it.

rubric.point: Median conditions and home price example

questions.stem: Employees' salaries are skewed (most earn ₹40k but the CEO earns ₹8L). Daily sales in a supermarket are stable. Best-selling t-shirt size is wanted. Choose a measure for each and justify.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** The choice follows the situation.

| Situation | Best measure | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Employees' salaries (skewed) | **Median** | Robust to outliers: most earn ₹40k but the CEO earns ₹8L |
| Best-selling product size | **Mode** | Shows the most frequent occurrence, e.g. size M t-shirts |
| Daily sales in a stable market | **Mean** | All values are comparable, e.g. a supermarket with consistent sales |

**Explanation.** In the salary case the mean would be inflated by the one very large pay cheque and mislead stakeholders, so the median is reported. The mode is the only sensible answer for a size category. For stable sales there are no outliers, so the mean, which uses every value, is best.

**Cautions.** Do not report the mean when outliers are present; watch for more than one mode; always state which average is used.

**Conclusion.** The measure must suit the data.
